---
title: "How .qmd files are changed"
---

Quartorium edits your `.qmd` file the way a careful co-author with a text editor would: it
changes the words that were edited and nothing else. Code, YAML, tables, equations and your
formatting habits survive byte for byte. This page explains how.

## The guarantee

> **A block that nobody edited is written back with exactly the bytes it had.**
> Only edited paragraphs are regenerated, and locked blocks (code, YAML, tables, equations,
> callouts, …) can't be changed from the browser at all.

So a Git diff of a review round shows the sentences people changed, not a reformatted file.
The test suite checks this: opening and saving an unedited document must return the
identical file.

## Step 1: split the file into blocks

The file is cut into top-level blocks at blank lines, using Quarto's own rules for fences,
divs, and so on. Each block remembers its exact text and the exact whitespace after it, so
joining the blocks gives back the original file.

| Kind | Example | In the browser |
|---|---|---|
| Prose | paragraphs, headings, lists, block quotes, `***` | **editable** |
| YAML header | `---` … `---` | locked; title, authors and date are shown |
| Code chunk | ```` ```{python} ```` … ```` ``` ```` | locked; its output is shown |
| Code block | ```` ```r ```` … ```` ``` ```` (not executed) | locked |
| Raw block | ```` ```{=latex} ```` | locked |
| Fenced div | `::: {.callout-note}` … `:::`, `::: {#fig-x}`, `::: {#refs}` | locked; rendered output is shown |
| Display math | `$$ … $$ {#eq-x}` | locked; rendered with KaTeX |
| Table | pipe or grid table, with its `: caption {#tbl-x}` line | locked; rendered output is shown |
| Shortcode line | `{{{< pagebreak >}}}`, `{{{< include _intro.qmd >}}}` | locked |
| Footnote / link definition | `[^1]: …`, `[quarto]: https://…` | locked |
| HTML comment | `<!-- note to self -->` | locked; shown as a hidden note |
| HTML block | `<div>`, `<figure>`, … at the start of a line | locked |

A prose block that turns out to contain something the editor can't represent (for example a
definition list or a line block) is locked as a whole, so it's shown and kept but can't be
edited.

Locked blocks are never sent back from the browser as text. The editor holds only their
*key* (a hash of their content). When a document is saved, the server puts the original
source back by key and refuses the save (HTTP 409) if locked blocks were removed, added or
reordered. A browser therefore can't change or inject code, even a modified one.

## Step 2: prose goes through Pandoc

Editable blocks are parsed with Pandoc (the one bundled with Quarto) into Pandoc's document
model, and from there into the editor. Many blocks go through one Pandoc call: each is
wrapped in a fenced div with a known id, `::: {#qtmseg-3}`, and the results are cut apart
again.

Pandoc's *smart* extension is switched off in both directions, so `--`, `"quotes"` and
`p. 3` are written back as typed, not as typographic characters or non-breaking spaces.

### Things the editor shows as chips

Inline elements that collaborators shouldn't retype are shown as small grey *chips*. A chip
carries its exact Pandoc representation and is written back unchanged. It can be deleted or
moved, but not edited.

| Inline syntax | Shown as |
|---|---|
| `@smith2020`, `[@smith2020, p. 3; @doe2019]` | the citation, e.g. "Smith 2020, p. 3; Doe 2019" |
| `@fig-mpg`, `@tbl-cars`, `@eq-energy`, `@sec-intro` | the cross-reference, e.g. "Figure 1" |
| `$E = mc^2$` | the formula, rendered |
| `` `r nrow(mtcars)` `` and other inline code | the code |
| images, raw inline HTML or LaTeX | the alt text or the markup |

Some syntax would be damaged by a Pandoc round trip, so it's wrapped as raw Markdown before
Pandoc sees it and comes back byte for byte:

| Protected syntax | Why |
|---|---|
| `{{{< meta title >}}}` and other shortcodes | Pandoc would escape `<` and `>` |
| `^[an inline footnote]` | the note's content would be rewritten |
| `[^long]` footnote references | the definition lives in another block |
| `[text][ref]`, `[ref]` reference links | the link definition lives in another block |
| `$$ … $$ {#eq-x}` inside a paragraph | the label would be separated |

The editor supports bold, italic, strikethrough, underline, superscript, subscript, small
caps, links, spans with attributes (`[text]{.mark}`), line breaks, headings, lists and block
quotes.

## Step 3: write back only what changed

When a draft is saved, each top-level paragraph in the editor still knows which original
block it came from. For every block, Quartorium compares the edited content with the original
in Pandoc's model:

- **unchanged**: the original bytes are used, including your line breaks, spacing and
  choice of `*` or `_`;
- **changed**: Pandoc writes the block as Markdown;
- **new**: written by Pandoc, separated by a blank line.

### Line breaks are kept

Pandoc writes a paragraph as one long line. If you wrap lines by hand, for example one
sentence per line, Quartorium puts the line breaks back wherever the words around them are
unchanged. A one-word edit shows up in Git as a one-line diff.

### A real example

A co-author changes "like" to "as" in a hand-wrapped paragraph that also contains bold
text, a citation with a page number, inline R code and inline math, and adds a comment. This
is the complete `git diff`:

```diff
@@ -16,7 +16,7 @@ format:

 Cars are *everywhere*, and **fuel efficiency** matters (a lot).
 This paragraph uses one sentence per line,
-and wraps lines by hand -- like many authors do.
+and wraps lines by hand -- as many authors do.
 See @fig-mpg for the main result and [@smith2020, p. 3; @doe2019] for background.
 Inline code `r nrow(mtcars)` gives the sample size, and $E = mc^2$ is famous.

@@ -82,3 +82,31 @@ Results are summarised in @tbl-cars and @eq-energy.

 ::: {#refs}
 :::
+
+<!-- quartorium
+{
+  "comments": [
+    {
+      "id": "c1",
+      "anchor": {
+        "quote": "fuel efficiency",
+        "prefix": "and ",
+        "suffix": " matters"
+      },
+      "author": "Anna Example",
+      "created": "2026-11-21T10:02:00.000Z",
+      "resolved": false,
+      "thread": [
+        {
+          "author": "Anna Example",
+          "created": "2026-11-21T10:02:00.000Z",
+          "text": "Define \"fuel efficiency\" -\u002d mpg or l/100 km?"
+        }
+      ],
+      "agree": [
+        "Bob Builder"
+      ]
+    }
+  ]
+}
+-->
```

The paragraph was rewritten by Pandoc, but the diff shows one changed line. `--`, the
citation and the inline code are untouched.

## Citations {#citations}

Citations inserted in the browser are written as ordinary Pandoc citations:

| In the picker | Written to the file |
|---|---|
| Smith 2020 | `[@smith2020]` |
| Smith 2020 and Doe 2019, page 3 | `[@smith2020; @doe2019, p. 3]` |
| *Name in the sentence* | `@smith2020` |
| Figure 1 | `@fig-mpg` |

The picker lists the entries of the paper's bibliography (from `bibliography:` in the YAML
header or the project's `_quarto.yml`; `.bib`, `.bibtex` and CSL JSON are supported) and the
labels of figures, tables, equations and sections in the paper. A new citation is accepted
only if every key is one of these, and the server rebuilds it from scratch, so nothing else
can be smuggled in through a citation.

Quartorium never changes the bibliography file. A missing reference becomes a comment of
type `reference` at that point in the text, for the lead author to add to the `.bib`.

## Comments {#comments}

Comment threads are stored at the very end of the `.qmd`, in an HTML comment:

```html
<!-- quartorium
{ "comments": [ { "id": "c1", "anchor": { "quote": "…", "prefix": "…", "suffix": "…" }, … } ] }
-->
```

- Quarto ignores HTML comments in every output format (HTML, PDF, Word), so comments never
  appear in the rendered paper.
- The prose has no markers in it. A comment is anchored by *quoting* the commented text plus
  a little context before and after it. If the quoted text occurs more than once, the
  context picks the right place. If the quoted words are edited away, the comment stays in
  the list with its original quote, marked as no longer in the document.
- `--`, `<` and `>` inside the JSON are escaped, so a comment can never end the HTML
  comment early.
- When there are no open comments, the block is removed completely.
- When a round is finished, resolved threads are removed (they stay in the Git history).

Fields: `id`, `type` (only for reference requests), `anchor`, `author`, `created`,
`resolved`, `thread` (each with `author`, `created`, `text`) and `agree` (names of people who
agreed).

### Files from earlier Quartorium versions

Earlier versions stored comments in a hidden `<div id="quartorium-comments">` with a JSON
code block and marked the prose with `[text]{.comment ref="id"}` spans. Such files are
migrated automatically the first time they're opened: the spans are removed from the text,
and the comments become quote-anchored comments in the new block.

## When branches are merged {#merging}

When main and a review round are merged (see [Main stays up to date](git.qmd#main)), the
paper is not merged line by line like other files. Quartorium merges it per block, with the
same splitting as above: blocks changed on one side are taken from that side, so edits to
neighbouring paragraphs never conflict. The comment block is merged per thread, so two
people commenting at the same time never produce broken JSON. Where both sides changed the
same paragraph, main's version is kept and the other version is attached as a comment.

## What is never changed

- The YAML header, code, tables, equations, divs, comments and shortcodes.
- Line endings (CRLF files stay CRLF) and the text before the first block.
- Any other file in the repository, including the bibliography and `_quarto.yml`.
- Blocks nobody edited, including their whitespace.
